notes.h: What the genetic code is (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A gene is a stretch of DNA, but a cell needs proteins, which are chains of amino acids. The genetic code is the translation key between the two, and the cell's machinery reads it to build each protein.
points: The genetic code is the set of rules by which the sequence of bases in DNA, copied into mRNA (messenger RNA, the working copy of a gene), is converted into the sequence of amino acids in a protein.

The code is read in groups of three bases. A codon is a sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid or for a stop signal. The matching three bases on DNA are called a triplet here, although some textbooks also call these codons.
Why three: there are 4 bases but about 20 amino acids. Reading one base at a time gives only 4 combinations, and two at a time gives only 16 (4 × 4), which is not enough.
Three bases at a time gives 64 combinations (4 × 4 × 4), which is more than enough to code for about 20 amino acids.
Of the 64 codons, 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons, which code for no amino acid and end the message.

The code is read by cellular machinery: the mRNA is read at a ribosome (the cell's protein-making structure) one codon at a time. Transfer RNA molecules bring the matching amino acids, which are joined in order. There is more on this in DNA Replication, Protein Synthesis and Mutations.
notes.tip: Define a codon as three bases on mRNA, not on DNA, and remember that a codon codes for one amino acid, not a whole protein. If asked why the code must be a triplet code, compare 4, 16 and 64 combinations against about 20 amino acids.

notes.h: Features of the code (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The code has a set of features that exams ask you to name and explain. Each one tells you something about how a cell reads a gene, or what happens when a base changes.
points: Start codon: AUG is the usual signal to start reading a gene's message. It sets where the groups of three begin, and it also codes for the amino acid methionine, so most new proteins begin with methionine.
Stop codons: UAA, UAG and UGA code for no amino acid. They signal the end of the protein, and the finished chain is released.

Non-overlapping and without gaps: the code is read three bases at a time from the start codon, each base belonging to only one codon, with no separators (like commas) between codons. Adding or removing a single base therefore shifts every codon after it, a frameshift mutation.
Degenerate, or redundant: most amino acids have more than one codon, because 61 codons code for only 20 amino acids. Glycine, for example, is coded by GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG.
Often only the third base differs between codons for the same amino acid, so some changes in a base still give the same amino acid and the protein is unchanged.
Specific, or unambiguous: each codon codes for only one amino acid. Degenerate means one amino acid can have several codons, but never the reverse, so the message is read the same way every time.

Universal: almost all living things, from bacteria to plants and humans, use the same code, with a few minor exceptions. In mitochondria, for example, UGA codes for tryptophan in humans instead of acting as a stop signal.

The shared code is evidence that all life shares a common ancestor. It also allows a human gene to be put into bacteria and read correctly, so that genetically modified bacteria make human insulin. There is more on this in Genetic Engineering.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain what is meant by a universal or degenerate code, and the role of start and stop codons. Give the meaning, then a consequence: universal means a human gene works in bacteria, degenerate means some base changes make no difference.

notes.b: A codon on mRNA does nothing by itself. Transfer RNA (tRNA) molecules act as adaptors, each reading one codon and delivering the amino acid it codes for.
points: An anticodon is a sequence of three bases on a transfer RNA (tRNA) molecule that is complementary to an mRNA codon. Codons are on mRNA and anticodons are on tRNA, never on DNA.
Each tRNA carries one specific amino acid, matching its anticodon. The anticodon pairs with the codon by complementary base pairing (A–U and C–G), so the right amino acid is brought for each codon.
For example, the codon AUG pairs with the anticodon UAC, and that tRNA carries methionine.
No tRNA has an anticodon for a stop codon, so when a stop codon is reached no amino acid is added and the chain ends.

Diagram: a short strip of mRNA divided into codons, for example AUG | CCU | AAA, with tRNA below, each anticodon paired to a codon and its amino acid attached at the other end. Draw tRNA simply, as a block or T-shape. Labels: codon, anticodon, mRNA, tRNA, amino acid.
notes.tip: Define codon and anticodon and state where each is found: codon on mRNA, anticodon on tRNA. RNA contains uracil (U), never thymine, so do not write T in a codon or anticodon.

notes.b: Exam questions give you a DNA or mRNA sequence and a codon table, and ask for the mRNA, the amino acids and the anticodons. Follow the same steps every time and the answer falls out.
points: Method: 1. Write the mRNA complementary to the DNA strand being read (A → U, T → A, C → G, G → C).
2. Split the mRNA into codons, starting from the start codon.
3. Find each amino acid in the codon table given in the question.
4. Stop at a stop codon, because no amino acid is added after it. 5. The anticodons are complementary to the codons.
Only AUG and the three stop codons need to be memorised; the other codons come from the codon table given in the question.

Worked example: the DNA strand being read is TAC GGA TTT ACT. The mRNA is AUG CCU AAA UGA, which codes for methionine, proline and lysine, then stops. The tRNA anticodons are UAC, GGA and UUU, with none for UGA.
Notice the anticodons have the same sequence as the DNA strand being read, with U in place of T.

Counting: each amino acid needs one codon of three bases, so a protein of 100 amino acids needs at least 300 bases of coding mRNA, plus three for the stop codon, giving 303. A stretch of 90 coding bases codes for 30 amino acids.
notes.tip: Use the table in the question rather than learning codons, and remember that mRNA and tRNA contain U, not T. In the worked example, only the starting DNA contains T, and the stop codon gets no anticodon.

keyTerms.definition: The set of rules by which the sequence of bases in mRNA is converted into the sequence of amino acids in a protein.
A sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid or a stop signal.
A group of three bases in DNA that corresponds to a codon on mRNA.
A sequence of three bases on tRNA that is complementary to an mRNA codon.
AUG, which signals where reading of the mRNA begins and codes for methionine.
One of UAA, UAG or UGA, which codes for no amino acid and signals the end of a protein.
A feature of the genetic code in which most amino acids are coded by more than one codon.
A feature of the genetic code in which almost all living things use the same codons for the same amino acids.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a codon and an anticodon.
questions.model: A codon is a sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for one amino acid or a stop signal. An anticodon is a sequence of three bases on tRNA that is complementary to a codon, so the tRNA brings the matching amino acid. For example, the codon AUG pairs with the anticodon UAC, and that tRNA carries methionine.

questions.prompt: Explain why the genetic code is described as a triplet code, and outline the role of start and stop codons.
questions.model: The genetic code is read in groups of three bases, each group a codon. Reading two bases at a time gives only 16 combinations, which is not enough to code for about 20 amino acids, but three bases give 64 combinations, which is more than enough. The start codon AUG sets where reading begins and codes for methionine. The stop codons UAA, UAG and UGA code for no amino acid, so they signal the end of the protein and the finished chain is released.

questions.prompt: A section of the DNA strand being read is TAC TTT GGA ATT. Using a codon table where AUG = methionine, AAA = lysine and CCU = proline, give the mRNA, the anticodons and the amino-acid sequence, and explain what happens at the last codon.
questions.model: The mRNA is AUG AAA CCU UAA. The anticodons are UAC, UUU and GGA. The amino-acid sequence is methionine, lysine, proline. The last codon, UAA, is a stop codon, which codes for no amino acid and has no matching tRNA anticodon, so no amino acid is added and the chain ends.
